tagline: Paul's most personal letter: a bruised apostle defends a ministry of weakness to a church he loves, and finds God's power at work precisely there.
overview:
Second Corinthians is the most autobiographical of Paul's letters and the most emotionally exposed. It comes out of a broken relationship. After Paul wrote 1 Corinthians, things between him and the church at Corinth got worse before they got better: a visit that went badly, a letter written in tears, and then rivals who arrived with impressive credentials and questioned whether Paul was a real apostle at all. This letter is Paul's answer. He explains his changed travel plans, rejoices that the church has turned back toward him, urges them to finish their share of a relief collection for poor believers in Jerusalem, and finally confronts, with painful irony, the teachers he calls the “super-apostles” (11:5).

Running through all of it is one conviction. The gospel of a crucified Messiah produces a ministry that looks weak by the world's standards. Paul carries “this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us” (4:7). He lists his beatings, shipwrecks, and sleepless nights rather than his successes, and he reports that when he begged to be rid of a “thorn in my flesh”, the Lord answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (12:7-9).

The letter also contains some of the richest theology Paul ever wrote, almost in passing: the new covenant of the Spirit (chapter 3), the hope of the resurrection body (chapter 5), the new creation, and the ministry of reconciliation, including the great exchange of 5:21, “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” It matters because it shows what Christian leadership is supposed to look like, and it refuses the celebrity model that tempted Corinth and tempts every age.
author: The letter names Paul as its author, with Timothy as co-sender (1:1), and it is one of the letters that nearly all scholars, conservative and critical alike, accept as Paul's own. Its vocabulary, its passionate and sometimes tangled sentences, and its detailed personal history fit what we know of Paul from his other undisputed letters and from Acts. The live scholarly question is not who wrote 2 Corinthians but whether it is one letter or a collection of several Pauline letters (or letter fragments) to Corinth that were later joined together. That question is set out under the date and in the reading notes below.
date: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:8), probably around AD 53 to 55. Second Corinthians comes some months to a year or more later. Paul says he left for Troas, found no peace because Titus had not arrived, and went on to Macedonia, where Titus finally met him with good news from Corinth (2:12-13; 7:5-7). The letter, or at least chapters 1 to 9, was written from Macedonia after that meeting, most often dated around AD 55 or 56. The outer frame of Paul's chronology is anchored by an inscription found at Delphi that places Gallio's term as governor of Achaia around AD 51 to 52, during Paul's first stay in Corinth (Acts 18:12). Scholars who think chapters 10 to 13 were a separate letter date those chapters either a little before chapters 1 to 9 (if they are the tearful letter) or a little after (if they answer a fresh crisis), in either case within the same one or two years.
setting:
Corinth sat on the narrow isthmus joining mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a port on each side, and grew rich on the trade that crossed it. The old Greek city was destroyed by the Romans in 146 BC and refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC. By Paul's day it was the capital of the province of Achaia, a place of new money, ambitious freedmen, public speakers, patrons and clients, and the Isthmian games. Status mattered, and people were judged by eloquence, connections, and appearance.

The church there had a turbulent history with its founder. Paul planted it around AD 50 to 52 and stayed about eighteen months (Acts 18:11). He then wrote an earlier letter that has not survived (1 Corinthians 5:9), followed by 1 Corinthians. Later he made what he calls a “painful visit” (2:1), apparently a humiliating confrontation in which someone in the church wronged him and the church did not defend him (2:5-11; 7:12). Instead of returning as planned, he wrote a severe letter “through many tears” (2:4) and sent Titus. The church repented, and Titus brought the news. But by the time of chapters 10 to 13, other teachers had arrived. They were Jewish Christians (“Are they Hebrews? So am I,” 11:22), carried letters of recommendation (3:1), were polished speakers, accepted financial support, and mocked Paul's unimpressive presence (10:10). Scholars debate who they were: some see them as law-observant missionaries like the troublemakers in Galatia, others as Hellenistic Jewish preachers who prized visions, rhetoric, and displays of spiritual power. A minority distinguish the “super-apostles” (the Jerusalem leaders, whom rivals invoked) from the “false apostles” of 11:13; most take the two phrases to describe the same group.
purpose: Paul writes to repair and secure his relationship with the Corinthian church, and through that relationship to protect their hold on the gospel itself. He explains why he changed his travel plans and wrote a painful letter, urges the church to forgive the man who had wronged him, and rejoices in their repentance (chapters 1 to 7). He asks them to complete the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem that they had eagerly begun a year earlier (chapters 8 and 9). And he confronts the rival teachers, not by out-boasting them but by boasting in his weaknesses, so that the church will stop judging ministry by worldly standards before he arrives for a third visit (chapters 10 to 13; 12:14; 13:1).
story: Second Corinthians belongs to the period of Paul's third missionary tour, narrated in Acts 19 and 20, when he worked for more than two years in Ephesus and then passed through Macedonia and Greece. Acts 20:2-3 records that he spent three months in Greece, most likely wintering in Corinth, which suggests the reconciliation this letter hopes for largely took place. It was probably there that he wrote Romans. The collection he urges in chapters 8 and 9 was carried to Jerusalem, where Paul was arrested (Acts 21), beginning the long imprisonment that ends Acts in Rome. In the larger story of the Bible, the letter shows the new covenant promised by Jeremiah and Ezekiel coming to life in real, flawed congregations, and it ties the church's present suffering to the hope of the resurrection and the new creation.
christ: The letter's picture of Christ is shaped by the cross. Christ is the one in whom “all the promises of God are ‘Yes’” (1:20), the image of God whose glory shines in the gospel (4:4-6), and the one who, though sinless, was made sin for us so that we might become God's righteousness in him (5:21). He is the rich one who became poor for our sake (8:9), the model for Christian generosity. Above all, Paul's own life of hardship and weakness is meant to mirror the pattern of Jesus: carrying around “the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed” (4:10), and finding that Christ's power rests on him most fully when he is weak (12:9). The letter teaches that the risen Lord still works through the shape of the cross.
reading: Read 2 Corinthians as real correspondence in the middle of a painful relationship. It is not a treatise; it moves by emotion as much as by argument, doubles back, and assumes events the readers knew and we have to reconstruct. Watch for irony, especially in chapters 10 to 13, where Paul plays the fool and boasts in order to expose boasting. Don't take the list of hardships as self-pity or the “super-apostles” language as simple praise. On the letter's unity, many scholars think it joins two or more letters, most often proposing that chapters 10 to 13 were once separate (because the tone shifts so sharply from joy to confrontation), sometimes that chapters 8 and 9 were separate notes about the collection, and sometimes that 6:14-7:1 was inserted from elsewhere. Others defend the letter as a single composition, pointing out that no manuscript ever circulated in pieces and suggesting that Paul turned to the stubborn minority at the end, or that fresh news reached him while he was writing. Readers can follow the letter's argument well on either view.

structure.title: Greeting and the God of all comfort
structure.summary: Paul opens by praising God for comfort in affliction, and tells of a crushing ordeal in Asia from which God delivered him.

structure.title: Changed plans and the tearful letter
structure.summary: Paul defends his integrity in changing his travel plans, explains why he wrote instead of visiting, and urges the church to forgive the offender.

structure.title: The ministry of the new covenant
structure.summary: A long reflection on Paul's ministry: a new covenant of the Spirit, treasure in jars of clay, the hope of the resurrection body, and the message of reconciliation.

structure.title: Titus brings good news
structure.summary: Paul returns to his story: Titus met him in Macedonia with word of the church's repentance, and Paul's anguish turns to joy.

structure.title: The collection for Jerusalem
structure.summary: Paul urges the Corinthians to complete their gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem, holding up the Macedonians' generosity and the grace of Christ who became poor.

structure.title: Boasting in weakness against the super-apostles
structure.summary: Paul confronts his rivals, reluctantly boasts as a fool of hardships, visions, and a thorn in the flesh, and prepares the church for his third visit.

themes.title: Power in weakness
themes.body: The letter's central paradox is that God's power is displayed through human frailty. Paul's hardships, his unimpressive presence, and his unanswered prayer about the thorn in his flesh are not signs that he is a failed apostle but the very place where Christ's power rests on him. The Corinthians, and his rivals, wanted a leader who looked powerful. Paul insists that the pattern of the cross governs Christian ministry.

themes.title: Comfort in affliction
themes.body: The letter opens with the God of all comfort, and the word comfort runs through its early chapters. Suffering is not denied or explained away. It is shared: Christ's sufferings overflow to his people, and so does his comfort, which then passes from one believer to another. Comfort in this letter is strength to endure, not relief from trouble.

themes.title: The new covenant and new creation
themes.body: Paul describes himself as a minister of a new covenant, written by the Spirit on human hearts rather than on stone tablets (chapter 3), echoing the promises of Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Those who are in Christ belong to a new creation (5:17), and God has given them a ministry of reconciliation that reaches out to the world.

themes.title: Generosity as grace
themes.body: Chapters 8 and 9 treat giving as a work of God's grace in people, not a tax or a fundraising scheme. The model is Christ, who became poor so that others might become rich. Paul stresses willingness, fairness between churches, and scrupulous honesty in handling money, and he sees the gift as a bond of unity between Gentile and Jewish believers.

themes.title: What makes a true ministry
themes.body: Against rivals who measured leaders by eloquence, letters of recommendation, pay, and spiritual experiences, Paul offers a different test: sincerity before God, the changed lives of the people served, faithfulness to the gospel of the crucified Christ, and a willingness to suffer for others. His own converts, he says, are his letter of recommendation.

keyChapters.why: The God of all comfort, Paul's near-death ordeal in Asia, and the declaration that every promise of God is Yes in Christ.
The ministry of the new covenant, written by the Spirit, and the unveiled faces that are being transformed into the Lord's image.
Treasure in jars of clay: the light of God's glory in the face of Christ carried by fragile, afflicted messengers.
The hope of the resurrection body, the new creation, and the ministry of reconciliation grounded in the great exchange of 5:21.
The grace of giving, modeled on Christ who though rich became poor, and the collection for the believers in Jerusalem.
Paul's vision of the third heaven, the thorn in his flesh, and the Lord's answer that his power is perfected in weakness.

parts.body:
2 Corinthians is a letter. Paul wrote it to the followers of Jesus in Corinth, the busy Roman city in southern Greece where he had started a church a few years before. It has 13 chapters.

It is the most personal of Paul's letters. In 1 Corinthians Paul answers a church's questions. In 2 Corinthians he opens his own heart. He writes as a pastor who has been hurt by people he loves, and who still loves them. He speaks of tears, of fear, of a time when he thought he would die, and of a weakness God would not take away. No other letter of his tells us so much about the man himself.

Something had gone wrong between Paul and the church. He had made a visit that went badly. He had written a letter that cost him tears. Then his friend Titus brought good news: the church had turned back to him. Paul writes this letter in relief and joy, and in some places in deep pain. He says so plainly: “For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you” (2:4).

The letter does three things. First, Paul explains himself: why he changed his travel plans, why he wrote instead of coming, and what kind of servant of Christ he is (chapters 1 to 7). Second, he asks the church to finish a gift of money it had begun for poor believers in Jerusalem (chapters 8 and 9). Third, he turns on rival teachers who had come to Corinth and set themselves above him. Against them he does something strange. He boasts, but only of the things that show he is weak (chapters 10 to 13).

That is the heart of the letter. Corinth admired strength, polish and success. Paul says God's power is seen most clearly in weak people. The Lord told him, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (12:9).

Some of the most loved lines in the Bible come from this letter: the God of all comfort, treasure in jars of clay, a new creation, the message of reconciliation, the God who loves a cheerful giver, grace that is enough. They all come from a letter written by a tired and wounded man to a difficult church.

The letter names its writer at once: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother” (1:1). An apostle is someone sent with a message. Timothy was Paul's younger helper, whom he had sent to Corinth before (1 Corinthians 4:17).

Nearly all scholars, of every kind, accept that Paul wrote it. The letter is full of his life: his travels, his hardships, his escape from Damascus in a basket, his vision and his ‘thorn’. Its long, tangled, heartfelt sentences sound like the Paul of his other letters. The real question scholars ask is not who wrote it but whether it is one letter or several of Paul's letters joined together. That question has its own part below.

Paul names Timothy beside himself, but the letter is plainly Paul's own voice. Much of it is written as ‘we’, Paul and those who worked with him. Yet again and again it turns to ‘I’, and those are some of its most personal lines. “I, Paul” (10:1), he writes, when he begins his last and sharpest appeal.

Paul had a long history with this church. He came to Corinth first and stayed a year and a half, earning his living as a tentmaker (Acts 18:1-11). He reminds them that the Son of God “was proclaimed among you by me and Silvanus and Timothy” (1:19). Silvanus is a fuller, Latin form of the name Silas, and most take him to be Paul's companion of that name in Acts (Acts 18:5).

So this is a letter from the church's own founder. That is part of why it hurts so much. The people now doubting Paul were people he had brought to faith. He calls them “my children” (6:13).

Paul wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia, the Roman province of northern Greece. The letter says so. Paul waited for Titus at Troas, a port on the coast of Asia Minor, and could not rest. “So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia” (2:13). There Titus came at last: “For when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest” (7:5). Paul then writes of the churches of Macedonia as the ones around him (8:1; 9:2). Which city he wrote from is not known. Philippi is often suggested, since it was one of his Macedonian churches, but the letter does not name the place.

When? Paul wrote 1 Corinthians at Ephesus, about AD 53 to 55. 2 Corinthians came later, after the painful visit, the tearful letter, and Titus's going to Corinth and coming back. Most date it about AD 55 to 56. As with every date in Paul's life, the years are worked out from a few fixed points, and the word ‘about’ matters.

One of those fixed points is an inscription found at Delphi in Greece. It shows that Gallio was governor of Achaia, the province around Corinth, most likely in AD 51 to 52, some say 50 to 51. Acts says Paul stood before Gallio during his first stay in Corinth (Acts 18:12). Counting forward from there gives the dates above.

What came next? Acts tells that Paul travelled through Macedonia and then came to Greece, “where he stayed three months” (Acts 20:3). Most think he spent those months in Corinth, and that he wrote his letter to the Romans there. If so, the visit Paul promises in this letter took place, and the church received him. Romans also says that “Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem” (Romans 15:26). Achaia is the province of Corinth. So the gift Paul asks for in chapters 8 and 9 seems to have been given.

Paul then took the gift to Jerusalem, where he was arrested (Acts 21). This letter belongs to the last years of his free travels, before the long imprisonment that ends the book of Acts.

parts.h: What happened between the two letters
parts.body:
2 Corinthians speaks of things that happened after 1 Corinthians, which Paul and the church both knew and which we have to piece together from the letter. Here is what it says, and what it leaves unclear.

In 1 Corinthians Paul planned to come to Corinth by way of Macedonia (1 Corinthians 16:5). His plans changed. He seems to have gone to Corinth sooner, and it went badly. He calls it a painful visit: “So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you” (2:1). Acts does not tell of this visit. But Paul later says, “This is the third time I am coming to you” (13:1). The first was when he started the church. The painful visit was the second.

During that visit someone in the church seems to have wronged Paul, or the church, and the church did not stand with him at first. Paul speaks of “the one who did wrong” and “the one who was harmed” (7:12). Who the man was is not known. Some have thought he was the man of 1 Corinthians 5, who was living with his father's wife. Many today think he was someone who opposed or insulted Paul during the painful visit. These notes do not choose.

Instead of coming again, Paul wrote a letter. “For through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart” (2:4). It is often called the tearful letter. Paul sent Titus to Corinth, and then waited, anxious, first at Troas and then in Macedonia.

What was the tearful letter? Here the evidence is thin. Many scholars think it is lost. Some think part of it survives in 2 Corinthians 10 to 13. A few have thought it was 1 Corinthians, but most find that 1 Corinthians does not read like a letter written through tears. These notes do not choose, as the book page on 1 Corinthians also says.

Then Titus came. “But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus” (7:6). The church had grieved, turned, and punished the wrongdoer. Paul now asks them to forgive him and take him back (2:6-8).

So Paul may have written four letters or more to Corinth: a first letter now lost (1 Corinthians 5:9), 1 Corinthians, the tearful letter, and 2 Corinthians. The Bible keeps two. What is plain is the cost. Paul stayed with this church through years of trouble, and he would not let it go.

Read 2 Corinthians straight through and you will feel a jolt at chapter 10. Chapters 1 to 9 end in warmth and thanks. Chapter 10 opens in sharp warning, and the last four chapters are full of hurt, irony and stern words. This change has led to an old question: is 2 Corinthians one letter, or several of Paul's letters joined into one?

There are three places where readers notice a seam. The first is the change of tone at chapter 10. The second is 6:14 to 7:1, a short warning about partnership with unbelievers. Paul's appeal ‘Open wide your hearts also’ (6:13) seems to run straight on into ‘Make room for us in your hearts’ (7:2), and the warning sits between them. The third is chapters 8 and 9, which both speak of the collection for Jerusalem, almost as if each began afresh.

Many scholars think 2 Corinthians joins two or more letters. The most common form of this view is that chapters 10 to 13 were once a separate letter. Some think those chapters are part of the tearful letter, written before chapters 1 to 9. Others think they were written after chapters 1 to 9, when fresh trouble broke out. Some think chapters 8 and 9 were once separate notes about the collection. Some think 6:14 to 7:1 was placed here from another letter, by Paul or by someone else.

Many other scholars read 2 Corinthians as one letter. They point out that no early copy of the letter has ever been found in pieces; every manuscript has it as one. They suggest that Paul wrote over a period of days or weeks, and that fresh news may have reached him before he finished. Or that he first spoke to the majority who had turned back to him, and only then turned to the rival teachers, who had not. On this view, 6:14 to 7:1 names the very thing that was keeping the Corinthians' hearts closed: their ties to the temples of the city.

These notes do not choose. The question is about how the letter came together, not about whether it is Scripture or whether Paul wrote it. On every view, the words are Paul's, and the church received them together as one letter. And readers can follow the letter's argument well on either view.

Some time after Paul left Corinth, other teachers came. In chapters 10 to 13 Paul answers them. He never names them, so we know them only through what he says.

Here is what the letter tells us. They were Jews, as Paul was: “Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I” (11:22). They carried letters of recommendation, letters from others vouching for them (3:1). They were polished speakers, and Paul was not: “Although I am not a polished speaker, I am certainly not lacking in knowledge” (11:6). They took money from the church, while Paul had preached “the gospel of God to you free of charge” (11:7). They compared themselves with others (10:12). They seem to have boasted of visions and revelations, which is why Paul, against his will, speaks of his own (12:1). And some in the church mocked Paul's weakness: “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account” (10:10).

Paul calls them, with bitter irony, “super-apostles” (11:5). Then he speaks more bluntly: “For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ” (11:13). He says they preach “a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed” (11:4).

Who were they? Scholars have long debated it. Some think they were teachers who wanted Gentile believers to keep the law of Moses, like the troublemakers Paul answers in Galatians. Others think they were Jewish Christian preachers who prized speaking skill, visions and displays of power, more than the law. Most take the ‘super-apostles’ of 11:5 and the ‘false apostles’ of 11:13 to be the same people. A minority think the ‘super-apostles’ were the leading apostles in Jerusalem, whose names the newcomers used, and the ‘false apostles’ the newcomers themselves. Paul speaks warmly of those Jerusalem leaders elsewhere, which is one reason most do not take that view. These notes do not choose.

What is plain is the contest. The newcomers measured a servant of Christ by the standards Corinth admired: speech, status, money, credentials and spiritual show. Paul does not try to beat them at their own game. He measures by the cross. And he names the problem as one of method, not of birth: he was a Jew himself, and his quarrel is with a way of ministry that serves the minister.

2 Corinthians falls into three large parts.

Chapters 1 to 7: the ministry explained and the friendship mended. Paul begins with praise to “the God of all comfort” (1:3), and with a time in Asia when he thought he would die. Then he explains his changed plans, the painful visit and the tearful letter, and asks the church to forgive the man it had punished (1:12 to 2:11). At 2:13 he is in Macedonia, waiting for Titus. Then the story stops. For more than four chapters Paul turns aside to describe what it means to serve Christ: a new covenant written by the Spirit (chapter 3), treasure in jars of clay (chapter 4), the hope beyond death and the message of reconciliation (chapter 5), hardships and an open heart (chapter 6). At 7:5 the story picks up exactly where it stopped. Titus arrives, the news is good, and Paul is full of joy.

Chapters 8 and 9: the collection. Paul asks the church to finish the gift it had begun for poor believers in Jerusalem. He holds up the poor churches of Macedonia, who gave beyond their means. He points to Jesus: “though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor” (8:9). He speaks of fairness, of honesty in handling money, and of joy in giving.

Chapters 10 to 13: the fool's speech. Paul turns to the rival teachers. He boasts, as they did, but he calls it foolishness, and he boasts of the wrong things: beatings, shipwrecks, sleepless nights, an escape in a basket, and a ‘thorn’ God would not remove. “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness” (11:30). He ends by preparing the church for his third visit, and with a blessing in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit (13:14).

Look for the words that run through all three parts. Comfort comes at the start. Grace runs through the money chapters. Boasting and weakness fill the end. They belong together. The God of comfort, the grace of the giving Christ, and power made perfect in weakness are one gospel seen from three sides.

Comfort in trouble. The letter opens with comfort. The Greek word, paraklēsis, means strength given by someone who comes alongside. Paul says God “comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God” (1:4). He does not say that suffering is good, or that comfort means the trouble goes away. He says God meets his people in it, and that comfort received is meant to be passed on.

Power in weakness. This is the heart of the letter. Paul carries the gospel like treasure in a cheap clay jar, “to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us” (4:7). He asked three times for his ‘thorn’ to be taken away, and it was not. The Lord answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (12:9). Paul's weakness is not proof that he is a failed apostle. It is where Christ's power rests.

The new covenant. Paul calls himself a servant “of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (3:6). God had promised through Jeremiah to write his law on his people's hearts. Paul says the Spirit is now doing it. The glory that shone on Moses' face was real. The glory of the Spirit's work is greater, and it changes people from within.

Reconciliation. To be reconciled is to be made friends again after a quarrel. Paul says God took the first step: “God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them” (5:19). The church carries that message, and Paul pleads, “Be reconciled to God” (5:20). It is also what Paul longs for with Corinth. The letter is itself an act of reconciliation between a pastor and his people.

Generosity. In chapters 8 and 9 Paul never orders the church to give. He calls giving a ‘grace’, a gift God works in people. The pattern is Jesus, who became poor to make others rich. The aim is fairness, not burden: “that there may be equality” (8:13). And the gift is meant to bind Gentile and Jewish believers together as one family.

Paul's mind is full of the Scriptures of Israel, and this letter shows it, even though it quotes them less than Romans does.

The biggest example is chapter 3. Paul reads the story of Moses coming down from Mount Sinai, his face shining, and covering it with a veil (Exodus 34:29-35). He sets the stone tablets of the law beside the promise of Jeremiah: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33). And he echoes Ezekiel: “I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).

Other quotations are set into the letter like stones in a wall. Paul quotes a psalm: “I believed, therefore I have spoken” (4:13), from Psalm 116:10. He quotes Isaiah: “In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you” (6:2), from Isaiah 49:8. In 6:16 to 18 he strings together promises from Leviticus, Ezekiel, Isaiah and 2 Samuel. In chapter 8 he recalls the manna in the wilderness (8:15; Exodus 16:18). In chapter 9 he quotes a psalm about the generous man (9:9; Psalm 112:9). He warns, “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (10:17), in the words of Jeremiah 9:24. He reminds them of Eve and the serpent (11:3). And he quotes the law's rule of two or three witnesses (13:1; Deuteronomy 19:15).

In several places Paul's wording differs a little from the Old Testament in the Berean Standard Bible. The BSB translates the Old Testament from the Hebrew. Paul, writing in Greek to Greek speakers, often follows the old Greek translation of the Scriptures that was in wide use in his day. The chapter notes point this out where it happens.

Paul reads the old Scriptures as pointing to Christ. He says, “For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (1:20). Every promise God made to Abraham, to David and through the prophets finds its yes in Jesus. For Paul, as for the church after him, the Old Testament is not left behind. It is read in the light of Christ, and it remains Christian Scripture.

2 Corinthians speaks a great deal about Paul's authority, and it has sometimes been misused. So it helps to say what it is not.

It is not a manual for church leaders to demand loyalty. Paul does defend himself, at length. But he defends himself as a servant, not as a master. He says, “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers with you for your joy” (1:24). He calls himself and his helpers “your servants for Jesus’ sake” (4:5). His authority, he says, was given “for building you up, not for tearing you down” (13:10).

And look at what Paul boasts of. Not his success, his crowds, his gifts or his visions, though he could have. He boasts of beatings, prison, hunger, danger and fear for the churches. “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness” (11:30). A leader who reads this letter and uses it to demand that people defer to him has read it upside down. Paul's rivals were the ones who “exploits you or takes advantage of you” (11:20). Paul says that is what the church should not have put up with.

It is not a promise that faithful people do not suffer. Paul was faithful, and he was crushed, afraid and sometimes near despair. The letter does not explain all suffering. It tells how God met one man in his.

It is not a fundraising letter. Chapters 8 and 9 do ask for money, but for the poor, not for Paul, who refused to take money from Corinth. Paul insists the gift be freely given, handled honestly, and carried by trusted people the churches chose (8:19-21). These chapters give no ground for teaching that giving money to God, or to a ministry, will make the giver rich.

And it is not a letter against the Jewish people. Paul was a Jew, and says so with pride (11:22). When he speaks of the veil in chapter 3, he speaks of his own people with grief and hope, as he does in Romans 9 to 11. The chapter note on 3:12-18 says more.

Read it as a real letter in the middle of a real quarrel. It is not a textbook. It moves by feeling as much as by argument. It doubles back. It assumes things the first readers knew and we have to piece together. Expect that, and it becomes easier to follow.

Read it in a sitting. It takes less than an hour. Read it aloud if you can, since it was written to be read aloud to the gathered church. Notice where the voice changes: joy, then grief, then warmth, then anger, then tenderness again.

Keep the story in mind. A painful visit. A letter written in tears. Paul waiting for Titus, unable to rest. Titus arriving with good news. Rival teachers who made Paul look small. Every chapter makes more sense when you know which part of that story it answers.

Watch for irony in chapters 10 to 13. When Paul calls his rivals ‘super-apostles’, he does not admire them. When he says he will speak ‘as a fool’, he means that boasting itself is foolish, and he is doing it only to show the church what it has been admiring. Do not read his list of hardships as self-pity. It is his answer to people who said a true apostle would look strong.

Notice the words that come back. Comfort and trouble. Boasting and weakness. Grace. Heart. Glory. Paul is not repeating himself by accident.

Let the letter read you. It asks who you admire and why. It asks whether you have been impressed by polish and power, and missed Christ in someone weak. It asks how you handle money, how you forgive, and how you carry pain. And it tells of a God who comforts the downcast.

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage. Chapters 1 to 7 are now in plain words.

hard.line: ‘We despaired even of life.’ Paul says he was given more than he could bear. What that means beside 1 Corinthians 10:13, and why no one should carry such a weight alone.
Forgive and comfort the man who was punished. Who he may have been, why discipline aims at restoring a person, and why forgiving is not the same as putting others back in danger.
‘The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.’ What Paul means by the letter, and why it is not a rule about reading the Bible loosely.
The veil over Moses' face and over hearts. Why this is not contempt for the law or for the Jewish people, and why the long misuse of these verses must be rejected.
The earthly tent and the heavenly house. What happens to a believer who dies, and how Christians read ‘at home with the Lord’.
‘God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf.’ Sin or sin offering, and how different traditions describe the great exchange.
‘Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers.’ What the yoke picture means, what Paul had in view in Corinth, and why it is no reason to leave a husband or wife.
‘Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor.’ Why Paul's appeal for money rests on the story of Christ, and what it does not promise.
‘False apostles.’ Who Paul's rivals may have been, and why his quarrel with them is about a way of ministry, not about who they were by birth.
A man caught up to the third heaven and to Paradise. Why Paul speaks of himself as ‘a man in Christ’, and why he will not say more.
The thorn in the flesh. What it may have been, why no one knows, and the answer Paul was given instead of healing.
‘Examine yourselves.’ Why this verse was not written to make anxious believers doubt without end.

words.line: Greek paraklēsis, strength given by one who comes alongside. With its verb it comes more often in this letter than in any other book of the New Testament. God is “the God of all comfort” (1:3).
Greek thlipsis, pressure, being pressed hard. Paul uses it of his own hardships, and pairs it with comfort. God comforts “in all our troubles” (1:4), not by taking every trouble away.
Greek kauchaomai, to boast, to take pride. More than half of its uses in the New Testament are in this letter. Paul's rule: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (10:17).
Greek astheneia, frailty, sickness, lack of strength. The world's reason to despise Paul, and the place of Christ's power: “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (12:10).

A covenant is a binding promise between God and his people. God promised a new one through Jeremiah, written on hearts. Paul is a servant “of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (3:6).
Greek katallagē, making friends again after a quarrel. In Paul, God is the one who reconciles and people are reconciled to him: “Be reconciled to God” (5:20).
Greek charis, a free gift and the goodwill behind it. In chapters 8 and 9 Paul uses it for God's kindness, for Christ's coming, and for the church's own giving (8:1, 8:6-9).
Belonging to Christ and sharing his life. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (5:17).
Greek arrabōn, a first payment that promises the rest will follow. God has given “the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come” (5:5; also 1:22).
Greek doxa, the shining greatness of God. It shone on Moses' face (3:7), shines “in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6), and is the “eternal weight of glory” still to come (4:17).
Greek diakonia, service. Paul's word for his own work and for the collection. It is the word for a servant's work, not a ruler's (3:6-9; 9:12).
The inner self that thinks, chooses and loves. The Spirit writes on “tablets of human hearts” (3:3), and Paul pleads, “Open wide your hearts also” (6:13).

timeline.what: Paul in Corinth for a year and a half with Silas and Timothy. The church begins (Acts 18:1-11).
Gallio is governor of Achaia, as an inscription at Delphi shows. Paul stands before him in Corinth (Acts 18:12).
Paul writes an earlier letter to Corinth, now lost (1 Corinthians 5:9).
Paul writes 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, in the province of Asia, planning to come through Macedonia (1 Corinthians 16:5-8).
A painful visit to Corinth (2:1), not told in Acts. Paul will later call his next visit the third (13:1).
Paul writes a letter “through many tears” (2:4), and sends Titus to Corinth. Many think the letter is lost; some think part of it is 2 Corinthians 10 to 13.
A crushing time of danger in the province of Asia, when Paul felt he was under “the sentence of death” (1:9). What it was is not known.
Paul waits for Titus at Troas, then goes on to Macedonia, where Titus meets him with good news (2:12-13; 7:5-7).
Paul writes 2 Corinthians from Macedonia, before coming to Corinth for the third time.
Paul spends three months in Greece, most likely at Corinth, and writes Romans there (Acts 20:2-3). Achaia has given to the collection (Romans 15:26).
Paul brings the gift to Jerusalem and is arrested in the temple (Acts 21; 24:17).

map.title: Corinth, Macedonia and the road between

places.name: Corinth
places.line: Where the letter went: “the church of God in Corinth” (1:1), the chief city of Achaia, where Paul had started the church and had made a painful second visit.

places.name: Philippi
places.line: The leading city of its district of Macedonia (Acts 16:12), where Paul had started a church. Paul wrote this letter somewhere in Macedonia after Titus met him there (7:5-7). Philippi is often suggested, but the letter does not name the city.

places.name: Troas
places.line: A port on the coast of Asia Minor. A door stood open for the gospel here, but Paul had no peace without Titus, and crossed over to Macedonia (2:12-13).

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: The chief city of the province of Asia, where Paul had worked for more than two years. He tells of hardships in Asia so heavy that he despaired of life (1:8). The letter does not say where in Asia.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.line: Where the poor believers lived for whom Paul gathered the collection of chapters 8 and 9. Romans names the city: the gift was “for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem” (Romans 15:26).

places.name: Damascus
places.line: Where, years before, the governor under King Aretas tried to arrest Paul, and he was let down in a basket through a window in the wall (11:32-33).

teaching.mapNote: Paul came from Ephesus, in the province of Asia, by way of Troas to Macedonia, and wrote from there to Corinth in southern Greece. The gift was to go to Jerusalem. Damascus is where, years before, Paul's life as a preacher nearly ended at its start (11:32-33).
